decks.title: Periodic Classification of Elements — Part 1: Early attempts and Mendeléev’s table
goals: Explain why scientists looked for a way to classify elements
Explain Döbereiner’s triads and Newlands’ law of octaves, with their limitations
Describe the basis of Mendeléev’s periodic table
State the achievements and limitations of Mendeléev’s table

slides.heading: Periodic Classification of Elements
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how chemists turned a growing list of elements into an orderly table, one attempt at a time. (This chapter is assessed through school-based activities and projects, not the board theory paper.)

visual.alt: Flow from many known elements to patterns, groups and finally a table that can predict

slides.narration: Namaste! Imagine a library where thousands of books are piled in a heap. Finding anything would be hopeless. Chemists in the nineteenth century faced a similar heap: dozens of elements, each with its own properties. In this lesson we follow three clever attempts to sort them, and see how the last one could even predict elements nobody had yet found.

slides.heading: Why classify elements?
slides.body_md: By the early 1800s, dozens of elements were known, and new ones kept being discovered. Sorting **similar elements together** makes their properties easier to study, remember and **predict**. Today **118 elements** are known.

rows: Study one element, learn about its whole family
No way to guess unknown properties
Properties can be predicted from position
New discoveries do not fit anywhere
New elements slot into a place

visual.alt: Table contrasting studying elements one by one with studying them in an orderly arrangement

slides.narration: Think of how a grocery shop keeps all the pulses on one shelf and all the spices on another. Once you know where one packet of dal is, you know where to find the rest. Chemists wanted the same thing for elements: put similar elements together, so that learning one tells you about its relatives.

slides.heading: Döbereiner’s triads
slides.body_md: In the early 1800s, the German chemist **Johann Döbereiner** noticed groups of **three** elements with similar properties. Arranged by increasing atomic mass, the **middle element’s atomic mass was close to the average** of the other two. He called these groups **triads**.

visual.alt: Table of three Döbereiner triads showing that the atomic mass of the middle element is close to the mean of the other two
visual.caption: Atomic masses are modern values, rounded to one decimal place.

slides.narration: Döbereiner spotted something neat. Lithium, sodium and potassium are all soft, very reactive metals. Write their atomic masses in order, and the middle one, sodium, is almost exactly halfway between the other two. The same trick worked for calcium, strontium and barium, and for chlorine, bromine and iodine. A triad was a family of three.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: testing a triad
slides.body_md: Calcium (40.1 u), strontium (87.6 u) and barium (137.3 u) are similar reactive metals. Do they form a Döbereiner triad?
bullets: Step 1 — Mean of the first and third: $\dfrac{40.1 + 137.3}{2} = \dfrac{177.4}{2} = 88.7$ u.
Step 2 — Atomic mass of the middle element, strontium: 87.6 u.
Step 3 — Difference: $88.7 - 87.6 = 1.1$ u, which is small compared with the masses.
Conclusion — the three are similar and the middle mass is close to the mean, so they form a triad.

visual.alt: Worked table: the mean of calcium and barium, 88.7, is close to strontium’s 87.6

slides.narration: To test a triad, check two things. First, are the three elements alike in their chemistry? Here they are. Second, add the masses of the lightest and the heaviest and halve the total. That gives eighty-eight point seven, very close to strontium’s eighty-seven point six. So this is a triad. Always state both checks in your answer.

slides.heading: Where triads fell short
slides.body_md: Döbereiner’s idea was the **first** sign of a pattern linking atomic mass and properties, but it could not classify most elements.

rows: First link between atomic mass and properties
Only a few triads were found
Most known elements did not fit into any triad
Some similar groups, such as nitrogen and phosphorus with arsenic, failed the mass rule

visual.alt: Table of the achievements and limitations of Döbereiner’s triads

slides.narration: Triads were a brilliant first clue, but a clue is not a system. Most elements simply did not belong to any neat set of three. Nitrogen, phosphorus and arsenic, for example, are related, yet the middle mass is far from the average. Chemists needed an arrangement that took in every element, not just a handful.

slides.heading: Quick check: predict a mass
slides.body_md: Use Döbereiner’s rule to predict the atomic mass of sodium from those of lithium and potassium.
slides.narration: Your turn. Take the mean of the two outer masses in the triad.

slides.heading: Newlands’ law of octaves
slides.body_md: In **1866**, the English chemist **John Newlands** listed the known elements in order of **increasing atomic mass**. He found that **every eighth element** had properties similar to the first, just as the eighth note of a musical scale repeats the first. He called this the **law of octaves**.

visual.alt: The lighter elements in Newlands’ order, seven to a row like the notes of a musical scale, so that lithium, sodium and potassium fall in one column and fluorine and chlorine in another
visual.caption: Every eighth element repeats the properties of the first, like the eighth note of a scale.

slides.narration: Newlands lined up the elements by mass and noticed a rhythm. Start at lithium and count: lithium is one, beryllium two, and so on until sodium, the eighth, which behaves very like lithium. Musicians know this pattern. In Indian music, sa, re, ga, ma, pa, dha, ni brings you back to sa, one octave higher.

slides.heading: Every eighth element repeats
slides.body_md: In Newlands’ order, **lithium, sodium and potassium** fall in one column, and **fluorine and chlorine** in another. For the **lighter elements**, the octaves group true families together.

visual.alt: Flow showing lithium, sodium and potassium each eight places apart in Newlands’ list and belonging to one family

slides.narration: Here is the octave pattern at work. Count eight from lithium, and you land on sodium. Count eight from sodium, and you land on potassium. All three are soft metals that react fiercely with water. For the light elements, Newlands’ rule really did bring families together.

slides.heading: Where the octaves broke down
slides.body_md: The law of octaves worked well only **up to calcium**. Among heavier elements, the pattern failed.

rows: Beyond calcium, every eighth element did not resemble the first
Assumed no new elements would be found
Later discoveries could not be fitted in
Two elements forced into one place
Cobalt and nickel were placed together, in the same column as fluorine, chlorine and bromine
Iron was placed far away from cobalt and nickel, which resemble it

visual.alt: Table of four limitations of Newlands’ law of octaves

slides.narration: Newlands squeezed the heavier elements into his octaves, and the families fell apart. Cobalt and nickel, two metals, ended up in the same column as reactive non-metals such as chlorine. Iron, so similar to cobalt and nickel, landed somewhere else. And when the noble gases were discovered decades later, they had no place at all.

slides.heading: Quick check: counting octaves
slides.body_md: In Newlands’ arrangement, which element is the eighth counting from lithium?
slides.narration: Quick check. Count lithium as the first, and keep going.

slides.heading: Mendeléev’s periodic table
slides.body_md: In **1869**, the Russian chemist **Dmitri Mendeléev** arranged the **63 elements** then known in order of **increasing atomic mass**, but he also grouped them by **similar chemical properties**, especially the formulas of their **oxides** and **hydrides**.

visual.alt: Part of Mendeléev’s scheme: groups one to seven with the general formulas of their oxides and hydrides, and one example element in each
visual.caption: R stands for any element of the group. Group VIII (iron, cobalt, nickel and others) is left out here.

slides.narration: Mendeléev wrote each element on a card with its mass and properties, and arranged the cards again and again. His key test was chemistry: how an element combines with oxygen and with hydrogen. Elements whose oxides and hydrides had the same kind of formula went into the same vertical column, called a group. He stated it as a law: properties repeat periodically with atomic mass.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: predicting formulas
slides.body_md: An element X forms a hydride with formula $\ce{XH3}$, and it is **not** in Mendeléev’s group III. Which group is it in, and what is the formula of its oxide?
bullets: Step 1 — From the scheme, the hydride $\ce{RH3}$ belongs to group III or group V.
Step 2 — X is not in group III, so it is in **group V**.
Step 3 — Group V oxides have the formula $\ce{R2O5}$, so the oxide is $\ce{X2O5}$.
Check — phosphorus fits: it forms PH₃ and P₂O₅.

visual.alt: Worked table linking hydride formulas to Mendeléev’s groups and the matching oxide formulas

slides.narration: Mendeléev’s formulas work like a code. Read the hydride, find which groups it fits, then read off the oxide. A hydride with three hydrogens could belong to group three or group five. Since we are told it is not group three, it must be group five, whose oxide has two atoms of the element and five of oxygen. Phosphorus is the real example.

slides.heading: Gaps for elements not yet found
slides.body_md: Mendeléev boldly left **gaps** where no known element fitted, and **predicted** the properties of the missing elements. He named them with the Sanskrit prefix **eka** (meaning "one"): eka-boron, eka-aluminium and eka-silicon. They were later discovered as **scandium**, **gallium** and **germanium**.

visual.alt: Table comparing Mendeléev’s predictions for eka-aluminium with the properties later measured for gallium: atomic mass about 68 against 69.7, and oxide and chloride formulas matching

slides.narration: This was Mendeléev’s masterstroke. Instead of forcing a wrong element into a place, he left it empty and said: an element belongs here, and this is what it will be like. Notice the word eka, borrowed from Sanskrit, meaning one. Eka-aluminium meant one place below aluminium. When gallium was discovered a few years later, it matched his predictions remarkably well.

slides.heading: Noble gases fit in neatly
slides.body_md: The **noble gases** (helium, neon, argon and others) were discovered **later**. Because they are very unreactive, they could be placed in a **new group** of their own **without disturbing** the existing order: another achievement of Mendeléev’s arrangement.

rows: Sodium and potassium in one group
Left gaps and predicted new elements
Values were rechecked to fit the pattern
Noble gases added as a separate group

visual.alt: Table of achievements of Mendeléev’s periodic table with examples

slides.narration: A good scientific arrangement should survive surprises. When a whole new family of gases turned up, argon, neon, helium and their relatives, Mendeléev’s table did not collapse. The noble gases simply formed a new column at the edge. That flexibility is one reason his table won wide acceptance.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: properties before mass
slides.body_md: Tellurium (127.6 u) is heavier than iodine (126.9 u). Strict mass order would put iodine first. Where should each go?
bullets: Step 1 — Iodine behaves like chlorine and bromine (the halogens); tellurium behaves like sulfur and selenium.
Step 2 — Following mass order would push iodine into the sulfur family and tellurium into the halogen family.
Step 3 — Mendeléev placed **tellurium before iodine**, so each sits with its own family.
Conclusion — he gave **similarity of properties** more importance than strict mass order.

visual.alt: Worked table showing that ordering by mass puts tellurium and iodine in the wrong families while ordering by properties puts each in its own family

slides.narration: Here Mendeléev trusted chemistry over arithmetic. Iodine is clearly a halogen, a cousin of chlorine. Tellurium is a cousin of sulfur. By swapping the strict mass order, he kept both families intact. Later we will see that the modern periodic table explains exactly why this swap was right.

slides.heading: Limitations of Mendeléev’s table
slides.body_md: Even Mendeléev’s table had problems that atomic mass could not solve.

rows: Hydrogen resembles both the alkali metals and the halogens
Isotopes of one element have different masses but the same properties, so they would need different places
Atomic mass does not rise in regular steps, so the number of missing elements between two known ones could not be predicted
Some heavier elements had to be placed before lighter ones

visual.alt: Table of four limitations of Mendeléev’s periodic table with reasons

slides.narration: Hydrogen is the odd one out. It has one electron like sodium, yet it forms molecules of two atoms like chlorine. Where should it go? Isotopes were an even bigger puzzle. Chlorine thirty-five and chlorine thirty-seven are chemically identical, yet a mass-based table would place them apart. A better basis than mass was needed.

slides.heading: Quick check: isotopes and mass
slides.body_md: Judge the assertion and the reason about the gaps in Mendeléev’s table.
slides.narration: Quick check. Are both statements true? Does the reason explain the assertion?

slides.heading: Summary: early attempts and Mendeléev
bullets: Döbereiner’s triads: the middle mass is about the mean of the other two; only a few triads were found.
Newlands’ octaves: every eighth element resembles the first; worked only up to calcium.
Mendeléev: increasing atomic mass plus similar oxide and hydride formulas.
Achievements: gaps with correct predictions (gallium, scandium, germanium); noble gases fitted in.
Limitations: hydrogen’s position, isotopes, irregular mass steps, mass order sometimes broken.

rows: Triads of similar elements by mass
Isotopes and hydrogen could not be placed

visual.alt: Summary table of the three classification attempts with their basis and main limitation

slides.narration: Let us recap. Döbereiner found families of three. Newlands found a rhythm of eight, which worked only for lighter elements. Mendeléev combined atomic mass with chemical properties, left gaps, and predicted new elements correctly. Yet hydrogen and isotopes showed that atomic mass was not the perfect basis. Part two reveals the better one.

slides.heading: Exam tips: early classification
bullets: For a triad, **show the mean** of the first and third masses and compare it with the middle mass.
For Newlands, state that the law worked **only up to calcium**, and give one limitation.
Mendeléev’s basis has **two parts**: atomic mass **and** formulas of oxides and hydrides.
Name the three predicted elements: eka-boron → scandium, eka-aluminium → gallium, eka-silicon → germanium.
Always pair a limitation with **why** it is a problem (for example, isotopes have the same properties but different masses).

rows: Newlands’ law works for all elements
Gaps were errors in the table
Gaps were deliberate places for undiscovered elements
The three must be similar, and the middle mass must be about the mean

visual.alt: Table of common mistakes about early classification with the correct ideas

slides.narration: To score well, be precise. Mendeléev used atomic mass, not atomic number; that came later. Remember that his gaps were a strength, not a weakness. When you write a limitation, add the reason in the same sentence. And for any triad calculation, show the working: add, halve, compare.

decks.title: Periodic Classification of Elements — Part 2: The modern periodic table and its trends
goals: State the modern periodic law and explain how it removes the limitations of Mendeléev’s table
Locate an element in the modern table from its atomic number
Predict trends in valency and atomic size across periods and down groups
Predict trends in metallic and non-metallic character

slides.heading: The modern periodic table
slides.body_md: Part 2 — one number, the atomic number, decides where every element sits and explains the patterns in its properties.

visual.alt: Flow from atomic number to electronic configuration to position in the table to properties

slides.narration: In nineteen thirteen, a young English physicist, Henry Moseley, showed that each element has a fixed number of protons, its atomic number. Arranging elements by this number cleared up every puzzle we met in part one. In this lesson you will learn to read the modern periodic table like a map, and to predict how elements behave from where they sit.

slides.heading: The modern periodic law
slides.body_md: **Modern periodic law:** the properties of elements are a **periodic function of their atomic numbers**. The atomic number (number of protons) is a more basic property than atomic mass, and it rises by **exactly one** from each element to the next.

rows: Added later as a new group

visual.alt: Table comparing Mendeléev’s table and the modern periodic table on basis, steps, number of groups and noble gases

slides.narration: Why is atomic number better than mass? Because it goes up in steps of exactly one: hydrogen one, helium two, lithium three, with no gaps and no surprises. So we know exactly how many elements lie between any two. And, as you will see, the atomic number decides the electron arrangement, which decides the chemistry.

slides.heading: Old problems, solved
slides.body_md: Arranging by atomic number removes Mendeléev’s main difficulties.

rows: Isotopes have the same atomic number, so they share one place
Atomic numbers are in the right order, so no swap is needed
Argon is heavier, but has the smaller atomic number

visual.alt: Table showing how arranging by atomic number solves the isotope problem and the order of tellurium and iodine, cobalt and nickel, and argon and potassium

slides.narration: Remember the tellurium and iodine swap? Tellurium has fifty-two protons and iodine fifty-three, so in atomic-number order tellurium comes first anyway. Argon and potassium are a similar pair. And isotopes, which differ only in neutrons, have the same atomic number, so they share a single box. Mendeléev’s instinct was right; atomic number explains why.

slides.heading: Layout: groups and periods
slides.body_md: The modern table has **18 vertical columns called groups** and **7 horizontal rows called periods**. Metals are on the **left** and in the **centre**, non-metals on the **upper right**, and **metalloids** lie along a **zig-zag** between them. Two rows (lanthanoids and actinoids) are placed separately below.

visual.caption: Hydrogen sits in group 1 but is a non-metal; it is a special case.

slides.narration: Here is the whole map. Columns are groups, numbered one to eighteen. Rows are periods, numbered one to seven. The wide middle block, groups three to twelve, holds the transition metals such as iron and copper. Notice how most of the table is metal. Non-metals crowd into the top right corner, with a staircase of metalloids along the border.

slides.heading: The first twenty elements
slides.body_md: Periods 1 to 3 have no transition elements, so groups **1, 2 and 13 to 18** are shown side by side. Each step to the right adds **one proton** and **one electron**.

slides.narration: Zoom in on the first twenty elements; you will meet these most often. Period one has only hydrogen and helium. Periods two and three each have eight elements, from lithium to neon and from sodium to argon. Potassium and calcium begin period four. Learn this small block well, and the trends will make sense.

slides.heading: Same group: same valence electrons
slides.body_md: Elements in the **same group** have the **same number of valence electrons** (electrons in the outermost shell). That is why they show **similar chemical properties**.

visual.alt: Table of the electronic configurations of lithium, sodium, potassium, fluorine and chlorine with their valence electrons, periods and groups

slides.narration: Look down group one: lithium, sodium and potassium each have one electron in the outer shell. Look down group seventeen: fluorine and chlorine each have seven. Chemical reactions involve outer electrons, so elements with the same outer arrangement behave alike. This is the real reason Döbereiner’s triads and Newlands’ octaves worked for some families.

slides.heading: Same period: same number of shells
slides.body_md: Elements in the **same period** have the **same number of occupied shells**. The **period number** equals the number of shells. Across a period, valence electrons increase **from 1 to 8** as the shell fills. The number of elements in a period depends on how many electrons the shells can hold.

visual.alt: Table of the seven periods with the outermost shell and the number of elements in each: 2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32 and 32
visual.caption: A shell can hold at most 2n² electrons, where n is the shell number (2, 8, 18, 32). From period 4 onward, inner shells also fill, so periods get longer.

slides.narration: Each period starts a new shell. Period one fills the first shell, which holds only two electrons, so it has just two elements. Periods two and three each have eight. Later periods are longer, eighteen and then thirty-two elements, because deeper shells can hold more electrons. So the shape of the table comes straight from electron arrangement.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: locating an element
slides.body_md: An element has atomic number 16. Find its period, group and valence electrons. Which element is it?
bullets: Step 1 — Fill shells 2, 8, 8: configuration **2, 8, 6**.
Step 2 — Three shells → **period 3**.
Step 3 — Six valence electrons; for 3 or more, group $= 10 +$ valence electrons $= 16$ → **group 16**.
Answer — period 3, group 16, six valence electrons: **sulfur**.

visual.alt: Worked table: atomic number 16 gives configuration 2, 8, 6, period 3 and group 16, which is sulfur

slides.narration: Two quick rules locate any of the first twenty elements. The number of shells is the period. For the group, one or two valence electrons give group one or two; three or more, add ten. Here, two, eight, six has three shells and six outer electrons, so period three, group sixteen. That is sulfur.

slides.heading: Quick check: find the group
slides.body_md: An element has the electronic configuration 2, 8, 7. What is its group number?
slides.narration: Your turn. Count the valence electrons and apply the rule for groups thirteen to eighteen.

slides.heading: Trend in valency
slides.body_md: **Valency** is the combining capacity of an element. Across a period it **rises from 1 to 4, then falls to 0**. Down a group it stays the **same**, because the valence electrons are the same.

visual.alt: Table of valence electrons and valency across period 3: valency rises from 1 to 4 and then falls back to 0 at argon
visual.caption: Valency = valence electrons (up to 4), or 8 minus valence electrons (from 5 to 8).

slides.narration: Sodium gives away one electron, so its valency is one. Magnesium gives two, aluminium three. Silicon shares four. From phosphorus onward, it is easier to gain electrons: phosphorus needs three more, sulfur two, chlorine one. Argon already has eight, so its valency is zero. Down any group, the valency stays the same.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: predicting a formula
slides.body_md: Element A has atomic number 20 and element B has atomic number 9. Predict the formula of the compound they form.
bullets: Step 1 — A: 2, 8, 8, 2 → two valence electrons → valency **2** (A is calcium).
Step 2 — B: 2, 7 → seven valence electrons → valency 8 − 7 = **1** (B is fluorine).
Step 3 — Cross the valencies: one A needs two B.
Answer — **AB₂** (calcium fluoride, CaF₂).

visual.alt: Worked table: valency 2 for element A and 1 for element B give the formula AB two

slides.narration: Positions give valencies, and valencies give formulas. Element twenty has two outer electrons, so it can lose two. Element nine has seven, so it needs just one more. One atom of A can therefore satisfy two atoms of B. The formula is A B two, which for real elements is calcium fluoride.

slides.heading: Atomic size down a group
slides.body_md: **Atomic size** is measured as the **atomic radius**, the distance from the centre of the nucleus to the outermost shell. Down a group, **a new shell is added** each period, so atomic size **increases**, even though the nuclear charge also increases.

slides.narration: Go down group one, and each atom has one more shell than the one above. Lithium has two shells, sodium three, potassium four. Extra shells push the outer electron farther from the nucleus, so the atoms get bigger: about one hundred and fifty-two, one hundred and eighty-six, and two hundred and thirty-one picometres.

slides.heading: Atomic size across a period
slides.body_md: Across period 3, atomic radius **decreases** from sodium (186 pm) to chlorine (99 pm).

visual.alt: Line graph of atomic radius against atomic number for period 3, falling from 186 picometres for sodium through 160, 143, 117, 110 and 104 to 99 picometres for chlorine
visual.caption: One picometre (pm) is a millionth of a millionth of a metre. Values are typical measured radii.

slides.narration: Now go across period three. The graph falls steadily, from one hundred and eighty-six picometres for sodium to ninety-nine for chlorine. Each atom is smaller than the one before it, even though it has more electrons. That seems strange at first. The next slide explains why.

slides.heading: Why atoms shrink across a period
slides.body_md: Across a period, electrons are added to the **same shell**, while the **nuclear charge** (number of protons) **increases**. The stronger pull draws the electrons **closer** to the nucleus, so the atom becomes **smaller**.

slides.narration: Sodium and chlorine both have three shells. But chlorine’s nucleus has seventeen protons against sodium’s eleven. Same shells, stronger pull: that is the rule across a period.

slides.heading: Metallic and non-metallic character
slides.body_md: Metals tend to **lose** electrons; non-metals tend to **gain** them. Across a period, the growing nuclear pull makes losing electrons harder, so **metallic character decreases** and non-metallic character increases. Down a group, outer electrons are farther away and easier to lose, so **metallic character increases**.

slides.narration: Being metallic is about how easily an atom gives up its outer electrons. On the left, atoms are big and the pull is weak, so electrons leave easily; these are metals. Moving right, the pull strengthens, and atoms would rather grab electrons; these are non-metals. Moving down, atoms grow, the pull weakens, and metallic character rises.

slides.heading: Metalloids and the nature of oxides
slides.body_md: **Metalloids** (semi-metals) such as **boron, silicon, germanium, arsenic, antimony, tellurium** and **polonium** lie on the zig-zag line and show some properties of both. Oxides follow the same pattern: **metal oxides are basic**, **non-metal oxides are acidic**.

visual.alt: Table of period 3 elements with their type, an oxide and its nature: sodium and magnesium oxides are basic, oxides of silicon, phosphorus and sulfur are acidic

slides.narration: Silicon is the classic metalloid: it looks shiny like a metal, but it is brittle and conducts electricity only partly, which is why it is used in computer chips. Oxides tell the same story as the table. Burn magnesium, dissolve the ash in water, and red litmus turns blue. Burn sulfur, dissolve the gas, and blue litmus turns red.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: comparing by position
slides.body_md: Three elements have atomic numbers 11, 13 and 19. Which is the most metallic, and which has the smallest atom?
bullets: Step 1 — 11: 2, 8, 1 (period 3, group 1); 13: 2, 8, 3 (period 3, group 13); 19: 2, 8, 8, 1 (period 4, group 1).
Step 2 — 19 is below 11 in group 1, so it is larger and more metallic than 11.
Step 3 — 13 is to the right of 11 in period 3, so it is smaller and less metallic than 11.
Answer — most metallic: **19** (potassium); smallest atom: **13** (aluminium).

visual.alt: Worked table comparing elements with atomic numbers 11, 13 and 19 by period, group, size and metallic character

slides.narration: Place each element on the map first, then apply the two arrows. Down a group, size and metallic character go up. Across a period, both go down. Potassium sits below sodium, so it is the biggest and most metallic. Aluminium sits to the right of sodium, so it is the smallest and least metallic of the three.

slides.heading: Quick check: the most metallic
slides.body_md: Which of these elements is the most metallic?
slides.narration: Your turn. Find the element farthest to the left and lowest down.

slides.heading: Summary: the modern periodic table
bullets: Modern periodic law: properties are a periodic function of atomic number.
18 groups and 7 periods; isotopes share one place; no mass swaps needed.
Period number = number of shells; same group = same valence electrons.
Valency: 1 → 4 → 0 across a period; same down a group.
Atomic size and metallic character: decrease across a period, increase down a group.
Metal oxides are basic; non-metal oxides are acidic; metalloids lie on the zig-zag.

visual.alt: Summary table of trends across a period and down a group in valence electrons, shells, atomic size and metallic character

slides.narration: Let us recap. Atomic number is the true basis of the periodic table. The number of shells gives the period, and the number of valence electrons gives the group. Across a period, atoms shrink and become less metallic. Down a group, they grow and become more metallic. With these rules, you can predict an element’s behaviour from its address.

slides.heading: Exam tips: modern table and trends
bullets: To locate an element: write the configuration, count the **shells** (period) and the **valence electrons** (group).
For groups 13 to 18 among the first 20 elements, group = 10 + valence electrons.
Always give the **reason** with a trend: "same shell, more protons" or "a new shell is added".
Valency is the number of valence electrons (up to 4) or 8 minus it (from 5 to 8).
Use oxides to show character: metal oxide turns red litmus blue; non-metal oxide turns blue litmus red.

rows: More electrons always means a bigger atom
Across a period atoms shrink as nuclear charge rises
Elements in a period have the same properties
Elements in a group have similar properties
Metallic character increases across a period

visual.alt: Table of common mistakes about the modern periodic table with the correct ideas

slides.narration: Examiners reward reasons. Do not just write that size decreases across a period; say the electrons enter the same shell while the nuclear charge rises. Keep group and period straight: shells give the period, valence electrons give the group. And when you discuss metallic character, link it to how easily an atom loses electrons.

notes.title: Periodic Classification of Elements — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Why classify? Döbereiner’s triads
sections.body_md:
*This chapter is assessed through internal (school-based) assessment, not the board theory paper.*

As more elements were discovered, chemists looked for a way to group **similar elements** so that their properties could be studied and **predicted** together.

**Döbereiner’s triads (early 1800s):** groups of **three** elements with similar properties. When the three are written in order of increasing atomic mass, the atomic mass of the **middle** element is roughly the **average** of the other two.

- Example: lithium (6.9), sodium (23.0), potassium (39.1): mean of 6.9 and 39.1 = 23.0.
- **Achievement:** the first hint that properties are linked to atomic mass.
- **Limitation:** only a few such triads could be found; most elements did not fit.

key_terms.definition_md: A group of three chemically similar elements in which the middle atomic mass is about the mean of the other two.

visual.alt: Table of three Döbereiner triads showing that the atomic mass of the middle element is close to the mean of the other two
visual.caption: Atomic masses are modern values, rounded to one decimal place.

sections.heading: 2. Newlands’ law of octaves
sections.body_md:
**Newlands (1866)** arranged the known elements in order of **increasing atomic mass** and found that **every eighth element** had properties like the first, like the eighth note of a musical scale (sa, re, ga, ma, pa, dha, ni, sa).

- Lithium, sodium and potassium fall in one column; fluorine and chlorine in another.

**Limitations**
- Worked well only **up to calcium**; for heavier elements the pattern broke down.
- Assumed only the elements known then existed, so later discoveries did not fit (for example, the noble gases).
- To keep the pattern, **two elements were put in one place** (cobalt and nickel), even in the same column as very different elements (fluorine, chlorine, bromine), while iron was placed away from cobalt and nickel.

key_terms.definition_md: In order of increasing atomic mass, every eighth element has properties similar to the first.

visual.alt: The lighter elements in Newlands’ order, seven to a row like the notes of a musical scale, so that lithium, sodium and potassium fall in one column and fluorine and chlorine in another
visual.caption: Every eighth element repeats the properties of the first, like the eighth note of a scale.

sections.heading: 3. Mendeléev’s periodic table
sections.body_md:
**Mendeléev (1869)** arranged the **63** elements then known by **increasing atomic mass**, and placed elements with **similar properties** in the same vertical column (group). His main test of similarity was the formulas of **oxides** and **hydrides**.

**Mendeléev’s periodic law:** the properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic masses.

**Achievements**
- Left **gaps** for undiscovered elements and **predicted** their properties: eka-boron (**scandium**), eka-aluminium (**gallium**), eka-silicon (**germanium**). ("Eka" is Sanskrit for "one".)
- Placed elements by properties even when this broke the mass order (tellurium before iodine), so families stayed together.
- The **noble gases**, found later, fitted in as a **new group** without disturbing the table.

key_terms.definition_md: A vertical column of elements with similar properties.
Sanskrit for "one"; Mendeléev’s prefix for an undiscovered element one place below a known one.

visual.alt: Part of Mendeléev’s scheme: groups one to seven with the general formulas of their oxides and hydrides, and one example element in each
visual.caption: R stands for any element of the group. Group VIII (iron, cobalt, nickel and others) is left out here.

visuals.alt: Table comparing Mendeléev’s predictions for eka-aluminium with the properties later measured for gallium: atomic mass about 68 against 69.7, and oxide and chloride formulas matching

sections.heading: 4. Limitations of Mendeléev’s table
sections.body_md:
- **Hydrogen:** resembles both alkali metals (one electron, forms positive ions) and halogens (forms molecules of two atoms), so it had no fixed place.
- **Isotopes:** isotopes of an element have **different masses** but the **same chemical properties**. A table based on mass would have to place them apart.
- **Irregular steps:** atomic mass does not increase in regular steps, so it was impossible to say how many elements might be missing between two known ones.
- **Mass order broken:** some heavier elements had to come before lighter ones to keep families together.

key_terms.definition_md: Atoms of the same element with the same atomic number but different atomic masses.

rows: It has one valence electron and can form a positive ion; it combines with chlorine and oxygen like sodium does
It needs one more electron for a full shell, forms molecules of two atoms (H₂, like Cl₂) and forms compounds with metals

visual.alt: Table showing why hydrogen resembles both the alkali metals and the halogens

sections.heading: 5. The modern periodic law and table
sections.body_md:
In **1913**, **Henry Moseley** showed that the **atomic number** (number of protons) is a more fundamental property than atomic mass.

**Modern periodic law:** the properties of elements are a **periodic function of their atomic numbers**.

- **18 groups** (vertical columns, numbered 1 to 18) and **7 periods** (horizontal rows).
- **Isotopes** have the same atomic number, so they share **one place**.
- Atomic-number order automatically puts tellurium (52) before iodine (53), cobalt (27) before nickel (28) and argon (18) before potassium (19).
- **Metals** are on the left and in the middle; **non-metals** on the upper right; **metalloids** (boron, silicon, germanium, arsenic, antimony, tellurium, polonium) on a zig-zag line between them.
- Groups 3 to 12 are the **transition elements**; the lanthanoids and actinoids are shown in two rows below.

key_terms.definition_md: The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom.
A horizontal row of the periodic table.
An element with some properties of metals and some of non-metals.

sections.heading: 6. Position and electronic configuration
sections.body_md:
The position of an element follows from its **electronic configuration**.

- **Same group → same number of valence electrons** → similar properties.
- **Period number = number of occupied shells.**
- Among the first 20 elements: 1 or 2 valence electrons → group 1 or 2; 3 to 8 valence electrons → group = **10 + valence electrons** (helium, with 2, is in group 18).
- Number of elements per period: **2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32**. A shell can hold at most **2n²** electrons.

**Example:** atomic number 13 → 2, 8, 3 → period 3, group 13 (aluminium).

key_terms.definition_md: Electrons in the outermost shell of an atom.
The arrangement of electrons in the shells of an atom, e.g. 2, 8, 1.

sections.heading: 7. Trends in the modern periodic table
sections.body_md:
**Valency:** across a period it rises from 1 to 4 and falls to 0; down a group it stays the same. Valency = valence electrons (1 to 4) or 8 − valence electrons (5 to 8).

**Atomic size (atomic radius):**
- **Across a period: decreases.** Electrons go into the same shell while the nuclear charge increases, so they are pulled closer.
- **Down a group: increases.** A new shell is added each time, so the outer electrons are farther from the nucleus.

**Metallic and non-metallic character:**
- Metals tend to **lose** electrons; non-metals tend to **gain** them.
- **Across a period:** metallic character **decreases**, non-metallic character **increases**.
- **Down a group:** metallic character **increases**, non-metallic character **decreases**.
- **Oxides:** metal oxides are **basic**; non-metal oxides are **acidic**.

key_terms.definition_md: The distance from the centre of the nucleus to the outermost shell of an isolated atom.
The tendency of an atom to lose electrons.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying Mendeléev arranged elements by atomic number (he used atomic mass and properties).
- Forgetting that Newlands’ law worked only up to calcium.
- Mixing up group and period: shells give the period; valence electrons give the group.
- Saying atoms get bigger across a period because they have more electrons.
- Saying metallic character increases across a period.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: correct option, term, group or formula.
- 2–3-mark answers: correct statement (1) + reason or example (1) + extra point or comparison (1).
- 5-mark answers: law or basis (1) + achievements or method with an example (2) + limitations or trends with reasons (2).
- Locating an element: configuration (1) + period and group (1).

Gallium, germanium, scandium.

cards.back_md: Henry Moseley, 1913.

cards.front_md: Groups and periods in the modern table?
cards.back_md: 18 groups and 7 periods.

cards.back_md: The number of valence electrons (so properties are similar).

questions.stem_md: In each of Döbereiner’s triads, written in order of increasing atomic mass, the atomic mass of the middle element is:

options.text_md: exactly double the atomic mass of the first element
the sum of the atomic masses of the other two
always the largest of the three
roughly the average of the atomic masses of the other two

questions.solution_md: Döbereiner noticed that the middle mass is close to the mean of the first and third — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Four sets of three chemically similar elements are listed with their atomic masses (u). Which set obeys Döbereiner’s rule most closely?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Mean of the outer masses for each set: $\dfrac{35.5 + 126.9}{2} = 81.2$; $\dfrac{14.0 + 74.9}{2} \approx 44.5$; $\dfrac{12.0 + 72.6}{2} = 42.3$; $\dfrac{16.0 + 79.0}{2} = 47.5$.

Step 2 — Only in the set 35.5, 79.9, 126.9 (chlorine, bromine, iodine) is the middle mass close to the mean (79.9 against 81.2). In the others the middle mass is far below the mean — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Newlands listed the elements in the order H, Li, Be, B, C, N, O, F, Na, Mg, Al, … . Counting lithium as the first, which element is the eighth, and so resembles lithium?

options.text_md: Fluorine
Magnesium
Sodium
Oxygen

questions.solution_md: Li (1), Be (2), B (3), C (4), N (5), O (6), F (7), Na (8). The eighth is sodium, a soft reactive metal like lithium — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Suppose neon had already been discovered when Newlands made his list. Placed by atomic mass, it would fall between fluorine and sodium. What would happen to his octave of lithium and sodium?

options.text_md: Sodium would become the ninth element from lithium, so the rule of eight would no longer hold for this family.
Sodium would still be the eighth element, because neon would be ignored as a gas.
Lithium would move to the same column as neon.
Nothing, because the law of octaves worked for all elements.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — With neon added, the list from lithium reads Li, Be, B, C, N, O, F, Ne, Na.

Step 2 — Sodium is now ninth, not eighth, so lithium and sodium no longer fall in one column: the octave pattern breaks — option (a). This is why the noble gases had no place in Newlands’ scheme.

questions.stem_md: Lithium (atomic mass 6.9 u), sodium and potassium (atomic mass 39.1 u) form a Döbereiner triad. Use the triad rule to predict the atomic mass of sodium (in u).
questions.solution_md: Mean of the outer masses: $\dfrac{6.9 + 39.1}{2} = \dfrac{46.0}{2} = 23.0$ u (the measured value is 23.0 u).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Newlands’ law of octaves applied to all the elements known in his time.

**Reason (R):** For the lighter elements, every eighth element in order of atomic mass had properties similar to the first.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is false: the law worked only up to calcium and failed for heavier elements. R is true for the lighter elements — option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Newlands compared the repetition of properties after every seven elements with the notes of a musical scale.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True. Just as the eighth note of a scale repeats the first, the eighth element repeated the properties of the first.

questions.stem_md: Groups of three chemically similar elements in which the middle atomic mass is about the mean of the other two are called Döbereiner’s ___.
questions.solution_md: They are **triads**.

questions.stem_md: Give one achievement and one limitation of Döbereiner’s triads.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Achievement:** triads were the first attempt to link the **atomic masses** of elements with their **properties**, showing that elements form families.

**Limitation:** only **a few triads** could be found; most known elements could not be placed in any triad, so the idea could not classify all elements.

questions.solution_md: Give one strength (first link between mass and properties) and one weakness (few triads).

marking_scheme.step: Achievement: first link between mass and properties
Limitation: only a few triads; most elements left out

questions.stem_md:
Class activity: Priya writes the elements in the order H, Li, Be, B, C, N, O, F, Na, Mg, Al, Si, P, S, Cl, K, Ca in rows of seven, as Newlands did.

(a) Which elements fall in the same column as lithium?

(b) Which element falls in the same column as fluorine?

(c) Why did this pattern fail when Newlands added heavier elements?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Sodium** and **potassium** (Li, Na, K are each seven places apart).

(b) **Chlorine** (and hydrogen above fluorine at the start of the column).

(c) Beyond **calcium**, every eighth element no longer resembled the first. To keep the rhythm, Newlands had to put **unlike elements together** (cobalt and nickel with the halogens) and two elements in one place, so the families broke up.

questions.solution_md: Count in sevens for (a) and (b); for (c) give the "only up to calcium" limitation with an example.

marking_scheme.step: (c) Fails after calcium; unlike elements forced together

questions.stem_md: Mendeléev arranged the elements in his periodic table mainly on the basis of:

options.text_md: increasing atomic number only
increasing atomic mass and similarity in the formulas of their oxides and hydrides
the number of valence electrons in their atoms
whether they were solids, liquids or gases

questions.solution_md: Mendeléev used atomic mass together with chemical properties, especially oxide and hydride formulas — option (b). Atomic number (a) was the later, modern basis.

questions.stem_md: In Mendeléev’s scheme, element E is in the same group as aluminium, whose oxide has the general formula R₂O₃. Which formula is expected for the chloride of E?

options.text_md: ECl
ECl₃
ECl₂
ECl₄

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — In R₂O₃, two atoms of R combine with three oxygen atoms (valency 2 each): total 6, so R has valency 3.

Step 2 — Chlorine has valency 1, so the chloride is ECl₃ — option (b).

questions.stem_md: In Mendeléev’s scheme, an element forms an oxide with the formula E₂O₅. What is the expected formula of its hydride?

options.text_md: EH₃
EH₅
EH
EH₂

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — E₂O₅ is the oxide of group V.

Step 2 — Group V hydrides have the formula RH₃ (for example PH₃ and P₂O₅ for phosphorus), so the hydride is EH₃ — option (a). EH₅ (b) wrongly uses the oxide valency of 5 with hydrogen.

questions.stem_md: Why did Mendeléev leave some places empty in his periodic table?

options.text_md: He could not decide the atomic masses of the elements already known.
He believed elements belonging there were yet to be discovered, and he predicted their properties.
Those places were meant for the noble gases, which he had already discovered.
He ran out of elements with similar properties to complete the rows.

questions.solution_md: The gaps were deliberate places for undiscovered elements such as eka-aluminium (gallium), whose properties he predicted — option (b). The noble gases were discovered later (c).

questions.stem_md: Tellurium (atomic mass 127.6 u) was placed before iodine (atomic mass 126.9 u) in Mendeléev’s table. What does this show?

options.text_md: Mendeléev gave more importance to similarity of properties than to strict order of atomic mass.
Mendeléev made an error in arranging elements by atomic mass.
Tellurium and iodine have exactly the same properties.
Mendeléev arranged elements by atomic number.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — In strict mass order, iodine would come first and fall among the sulfur family.

Step 2 — Iodine clearly resembles chlorine and bromine, so Mendeléev reversed the order to keep each element with its family — option (a). It was a deliberate choice, not a mistake (b); atomic number was not yet known (d).

questions.stem_md: Chlorine has two isotopes, of masses 35 u and 37 u. Why were isotopes a problem for Mendeléev’s periodic table?

options.text_md: Isotopes have different chemical properties, so they belong to different groups.
Isotopes have different atomic numbers, so they cannot share a place.
Arranged by mass, the two isotopes would need different places, although they have the same chemical properties.
Mendeléev’s table had no place for chlorine.

questions.solution_md: Isotopes differ only in mass; their chemistry is the same. A mass-based table would separate them, though they should sit together — option (c). Isotopes share the same atomic number (b).

questions.stem_md: Helium, neon and argon were discovered after Mendeléev made his table. How were they fitted in?

options.text_md: Into the gaps that Mendeléev had left for eka-elements
Into the same group as the halogens
As a separate new group, without disturbing the order of the other elements
They could not be fitted in, so his table was abandoned

questions.solution_md: Being very unreactive, the noble gases formed a new group of their own; the rest of the table was unchanged — option (c). The gaps (a) were filled by gallium, scandium and germanium.

questions.stem_md: Gallium forms an oxide with the formula Ga₂O₃, just as Mendeléev predicted for eka-aluminium. Taking the valency of oxygen as 2, what is the valency of gallium?
questions.solution_md: Three oxygen atoms supply $3 \times 2 = 6$ units of combining capacity, shared by two gallium atoms: $\dfrac{6}{2} = 3$.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Mendeléev’s periodic table helped in the discovery of new elements.

**Reason (R):** Mendeléev left gaps in his table and predicted the properties of the elements that would fill them.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true. Because he predicted the properties of the missing elements, chemists knew what to look for, and gallium, scandium and germanium were found — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In Mendeléev’s table, tellurium is placed before iodine.

**Reason (R):** Tellurium has a greater atomic mass than iodine.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but the greater mass of tellurium is not why it comes first; in fact it goes against the mass order. Tellurium was placed first so that iodine could sit with the halogens — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Mendeléev’s table gave hydrogen a fixed position that settled whether it belongs with the alkali metals or the halogens.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False. Hydrogen resembles both alkali metals and halogens, and Mendeléev could not fix its position; this is one of the limitations of his table.

questions.stem_md: Mendeléev named undiscovered elements using the Sanskrit prefix ___, meaning "one", as in the name he gave to gallium before it was found.
questions.solution_md: The prefix is **eka**: gallium was eka-aluminium.

questions.stem_md: Match each group of Mendeléev’s table in Column A with the general formula of its oxide in Column B.

options.text_md: Group I
Group II
Group IV
Group VII

questions.solution_md: Group I → R₂O (1 → r); group II → RO (2 → p); group IV → RO₂ (3 → s); group VII → R₂O₇ (4 → q). In each, twice the oxygen count divided by the R count equals the group number.

questions.stem_md: State two achievements of Mendeléev’s periodic table, with an example of each.

answer.model_answer_md:
(1) He left **gaps** for undiscovered elements and **predicted** their properties; for example, eka-aluminium was later found as **gallium** with matching properties.

(2) The **noble gases**, discovered later, could be placed as a **new group** without disturbing the existing order.

questions.solution_md: Name two strengths and give a matching example for each.

marking_scheme.step: Gaps and correct predictions, with example
Second achievement (noble gases fitted in, or families kept together), with example

questions.stem_md: Why were isotopes a problem for Mendeléev’s periodic table? How does the modern periodic table remove this problem?

answer.model_answer_md: Isotopes of an element have **different atomic masses** but the **same chemical properties**. In a table based on atomic mass they would need separate places. In the modern table, elements are arranged by **atomic number**, and isotopes have the **same atomic number**, so they share one place.

questions.solution_md: State the problem (mass differs, properties same) and the solution (same atomic number).

marking_scheme.step: Solution: same atomic number, one place

questions.stem_md:
Tellurium has atomic mass 127.6 u and atomic number 52; iodine has atomic mass 126.9 u and atomic number 53. Iodine resembles chlorine and bromine.

(a) Where would strict mass order place these two elements?

(b) What did Mendeléev do, and why?

(c) How does the modern periodic law show that he was right?

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Iodine, being lighter, would come **before** tellurium, and would land in the family of sulfur and selenium, while tellurium would go with the halogens.

(b) Mendeléev placed **tellurium first**, breaking the mass order, so that **iodine** stays with **chlorine and bromine**, whose properties it shares.

(c) In order of **atomic number**, tellurium (52) comes before iodine (53) anyway, so both sit in the right families without any swap.

questions.solution_md: Compare mass order with atomic-number order and link each to the families.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Mass order puts iodine first, in the wrong family
(b) Swapped to keep iodine with the halogens
(c) Atomic numbers 52 < 53 give the right order

questions.stem_md:
(a) On what basis did Mendeléev arrange the elements?

(b) Describe two achievements of his periodic table.

(c) Explain three of its limitations.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) He arranged the elements in order of **increasing atomic mass**, and placed elements with **similar properties**, judged mainly by the formulas of their **oxides and hydrides**, in the same group.

(b) He left **gaps** for undiscovered elements and predicted their properties; eka-aluminium and eka-silicon were later found as **gallium** and **germanium** with matching properties. The **noble gases**, found later, fitted in as a new group without disturbing the table.

(c) **Hydrogen** resembles both alkali metals and halogens, so it had no fixed place. **Isotopes** have different masses but the same properties, so a mass-based table would place them apart. Atomic masses do not rise in **regular steps**, so the number of missing elements between two known ones could not be predicted.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1 — Basis: mass plus oxide and hydride formulas.

Step 2 — Two achievements with examples.

Step 3 — Three limitations, each with its reason.

marking_scheme.step: (a) Basis: atomic mass and similar properties

questions.stem_md: According to the modern periodic law, the properties of elements are a periodic function of their:

options.text_md: atomic numbers
atomic masses
densities
numbers of neutrons

questions.solution_md: The modern law, based on Moseley’s work, uses the atomic number — option (a). Atomic mass (b) was Mendeléev’s basis.

questions.stem_md: An element has the electronic configuration 2, 8, 2. Where is it in the modern periodic table?

options.text_md: Period 2, group 3
Period 3, group 2
Period 3, group 12
Period 2, group 12

questions.solution_md: Three shells → period 3. Two valence electrons → group 2 — option (b). It is magnesium.

questions.stem_md: Which atomic number belongs to an element in the same group as the element with atomic number 9?

questions.stem_md:
(a) State the modern periodic law.

(b) Explain how the period and group of an element are found from its electronic configuration, using the element with atomic number 19 as an example.

(c) How do atomic size and metallic character change across a period and down a group? Give reasons.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The properties of elements are a **periodic function of their atomic numbers**.

(b) The number of occupied **shells** gives the **period**, and the number of **valence electrons** gives the **group**. Atomic number 19 → **2, 8, 8, 1**: four shells, so **period 4**; one valence electron, so **group 1** (potassium).

(c) **Across a period**, electrons enter the same shell while the nuclear charge rises, so they are pulled closer: atomic size **decreases**, and electrons are lost less easily, so metallic character **decreases**. **Down a group**, a new shell is added each time, so atomic size **increases**; the outer electrons are farther from the nucleus and easier to lose, so metallic character **increases**.

Step 2 — Shells give the period, valence electrons the group; apply to 19.

Step 3 — Give both trends with reasons.

questions.stem_md: Compare Mendeléev’s periodic table with the modern periodic table under these headings: (a) basis of arrangement, (b) number of groups and the place of the noble gases, (c) position of isotopes, (d) order of elements such as tellurium and iodine, (e) one problem that remains in both.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Mendeléev: **increasing atomic mass** and similar properties. Modern: **increasing atomic number**.

(b) Mendeléev: **eight** groups (I to VIII), with the noble gases added later as a new group. Modern: **18** groups, with the noble gases in **group 18**.

(c) Mendeléev: isotopes, having different masses, would need **different places**. Modern: isotopes have the same atomic number, so they share **one place**.

(d) Mendeléev had to place tellurium (heavier) **before** iodine against the mass order. Modern: tellurium (52) comes before iodine (53) **naturally**.

(e) The position of **hydrogen**, which resembles both alkali metals and halogens, is still a special case.

questions.stem_md: Describe how the classification of elements developed through the work of (a) Döbereiner, (b) Newlands and (c) Mendeléev. For each, give the main idea and one limitation.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Döbereiner** grouped similar elements in **triads**; in each, the middle atomic mass was about the mean of the other two (lithium, sodium, potassium). **Limitation:** only a few triads could be found.

(b) **Newlands** arranged elements by increasing atomic mass and found that **every eighth element** resembled the first (law of octaves). **Limitation:** it worked only up to **calcium**.

(c) **Mendeléev** arranged elements by increasing atomic mass and **similar properties** (oxide and hydride formulas), left **gaps** and predicted new elements. **Limitation:** he could not place **isotopes** or fix the position of **hydrogen**.

questions.solution_md: Give each scientist’s idea with an example and one limitation, in order of time.
